summary.text: For \(1\le k<60\), explicit prime decompositions handle the finite range. For \(k\ge60\), set \(n=2k+1\); the assumed nonzero determinant forces some matrix entry to be \(1\), and its two defining primes sum to \(2n=4k+2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(A(n)\) denote the sequence term in question. Thus, for each positive integer \(n\), form the \(n\times n\) integer matrix \(M_n\), whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and define
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the differences may be regarded as natural-number differences: because \(0\le i,j<n\), we have \(j<n\le n+i\) and \(i<n\le n+j\), so neither subtraction is truncated. By definition,
\[
A(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing assertion:
\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad A(n)\ne0.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that for every integer \(k>0\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First dispose of the finite range \(1\le k<60\). The following table gives, for each such \(k\), two primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=4k+2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&(p,q)& &k&(p,q)&\\ \hline
1&(3,3)&&21&(3,83)&&41&(3,163)\\
2&(3,7)&&22&(7,83)&&42&(3,167)\\
3&(3,11)&&23&(5,89)&&43&(7,167)\\
4&(5,13)&&24&(19,79)&&44&(5,173)\\
5&(3,19)&&25&(5,97)&&45&(3,179)\\
6&(3,23)&&26&(3,103)&&46&(5,181)\\
7&(7,23)&&27&(3,107)&&47&(11,179)\\
8&(3,31)&&28&(5,109)&&48&(3,191)\\
9&(7,31)&&29&(5,113)&&49&(5,193)\\
10&(5,37)&&30&(13,109)&&50&(3,199)\\
11&(3,43)&&31&(13,113)&&51&(7,199)\\
12&(3,47)&&32&(3,127)&&52&(11,199)\\
13&(7,47)&&33&(3,131)&&53&(3,211)\\
14&(5,53)&&34&(7,131)&&54&(7,211)\\
15&(3,59)&&35&(3,139)&&55&(11,211)\\
16&(5,61)&&36&(7,139)&&56&(3,223)\\
17&(3,67)&&37&(11,139)&&57&(3,227)\\
18&(3,71)&&38&(3,151)&&58&(5,229)\\
19&(5,73)&&39&(7,151)&&59&(5,233)\\
20&(3,79)&&40&(5,157)&&&
\end{array}
\]
For every row, direct addition gives the required value \(4k+2\). Every number appearing in the pairs is prime; this is checked by trial division by primes no larger than its square root (the largest number in the table is \(233\), so only divisors through \(13\) need be considered). Thus the desired conclusion holds throughout the finite range \(1\le k<60\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge60\). Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]
Consequently, hypothesis (1) gives
\[
\det(M_n)=A(n)\ne0.
\tag{2}
\]

We claim that \(M_n\) has at least one nonzero entry. Indeed, if every entry were zero, then \(M_n\) would be the zero matrix. Since \(n>0\), the determinant of this zero \(n\times n\) matrix is zero, contradicting (2). Hence there are indices \(i,j\), with
\[
0\le i<n,\qquad 0\le j<n,
\]
such that
\[
(M_n)_{ij}\ne0.
\]
Every entry of \(M_n\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). By its defining condition, a nonzero entry must therefore equal \(1\), and the two numbers
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]
are both prime.

For completeness, the index bounds ensure these are genuine nonnegative differences. Namely, \(j<n\le n+i\), so \(j\le n+i\), and likewise \(i<n\le n+j\), so \(i\le n+j\). We may therefore add the two expressions without any issue from natural-number subtraction:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p+q
  &= (n+i-j)+(n+j-i)\\
  &=2n\\
  &=2(2k+1)\\
  &=4k+2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(4k+2\) is the sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(q\).

The finite table covers every positive \(k<60\), while the determinant argument covers every \(k\ge60\). Therefore, under the assumption that \(A(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.
